compound.title: Compound interest calculator
compound.intro: Put in what you have now, what you can add each month and a yearly interest rate. You'll see what it could grow to, and how much of that is money you never paid in.

inputs.rateHelp: Use the AER on a savings account, or a cautious long-term return for investments.

results.heading: After {{years}} years
results.share: {{percent}}% of the final balance is interest.

compound.invalid: Enter amounts of 0 or more, a rate between 0 and 30%, and 1 to 60 years.

how.heading: How compound interest works
how.p1: Simple interest is paid only on the money you put in. Compound interest is also paid on the interest you've already earned, so each year the pot that earns interest is a little bigger than the year before.
how.p2: This calculator compounds monthly: each month, a twelfth of the yearly rate is added to the balance, then your deposit goes in. That's close to how most UK savings accounts and investment platforms work, though some pay interest only once a year.
how.formula: With a monthly rate r (yearly rate ÷ 12) and n months, a starting sum P grows to P × (1 + r)ⁿ, and a monthly deposit m grows to m × ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1) ÷ r.

example.heading: An example
example.body: £150 a month for 20 years is £36,000 paid in. At 7% a year, compounded monthly, it grows to about £78,000, so more than half the final pot is interest. At 3% it reaches about £49,000. Time and rate matter more than the size of each deposit.

caveats.heading: What the calculator leaves out
caveats.body: Rates change, and investment returns go down as well as up, so treat the result as an illustration, not a forecast. It ignores tax: interest above your Personal Savings Allowance is taxable unless it sits in an ISA. It also ignores inflation, which shrinks what the final sum will buy.

savingsGoal.title: Savings goal calculator
savingsGoal.intro: Set a target — an emergency fund, a house deposit, a trip — and add what you've already saved. See how much to put away each month to get there on time, or how long your current monthly amount will take.

savingsGoal.invalid: Enter a goal above 0, amounts of 0 or more, a rate between 0 and 30%, and 1 to 600 months.

how.heading: How the calculator works
how.p1: It starts from what you've already saved and adds your monthly amount at the end of each month. Interest is added monthly at a twelfth of the yearly rate, on everything saved so far — including interest you've already earned.
how.p2: To find the monthly amount, it works out what your current savings will grow to by the deadline, then the deposit that covers the rest, rounded up to the nearest pound. To find the time, it steps forward month by month until the balance reaches the goal.

example.heading: An example
example.body: Say you want a £6,000 emergency fund in two years, starting from nothing. Without interest that's £250 a month. In an easy-access account paying 4%, about £241 a month gets you there, because interest covers the rest. Give yourself three years and it drops to about £157.

tips.heading: Making the goal stick
tips.body: Set up a standing order for payday, so the saving happens before you can spend it. Keep the money in a separate account, ideally one that pays interest, and check in every few months. If your pay or the rate changes, rerun the numbers and adjust the amount rather than giving up on the goal.

caveats.heading: What the calculator leaves out
caveats.body: Savings rates change, so treat the result as a plan, not a promise. It ignores tax: interest above your Personal Savings Allowance is taxable unless the money sits in an ISA. It also ignores inflation — if your goal is a price that will rise, like a house deposit, aim a little higher.

faq.q1: How much should I save each month?
faq.a1: Work back from the goal: divide what's left by the months you have, then let interest trim it a little. If the answer doesn't fit your budget, give yourself more time rather than skipping months — a smaller amount you keep up beats a bigger one you abandon.
faq.q2: How big should an emergency fund be?
faq.a2: A common rule of thumb is three to six months of essential costs: rent, bills, food and travel. Start with one month as a first goal, then build from there.
faq.q3: Where should I keep money I'm saving for a goal?
faq.a3: For goals a few years away, an easy-access savings account or a cash ISA keeps the money safe and earning interest. Investing suits goals five or more years away, because prices can fall in the short term.
faq.a4: Yes. Interest is added monthly at the rate you enter. Set the rate to 0 to see the figure without it.

budget.title: 50/30/20 budget calculator
budget.intro: Enter what lands in your account each month after tax. The 50/30/20 rule splits it into needs, wants and savings — and if your essentials already cost more than half, you'll see where the difference has to come from.

inputs.incomeHelp: Your pay after tax, National Insurance and pension contributions.

budget.invalid: Enter take-home pay above 0, and essentials of 0 or more.

how.heading: How the 50/30/20 rule works
how.p1: The rule was popularised by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi in their 2005 book All Your Worth. It splits take-home pay three ways: half for the things you must pay, 30% for the things you choose, and 20% for your future.
how.p2: Needs are costs you can't easily skip: rent or mortgage, council tax, energy, food shopping, getting to work, insurance and minimum debt payments. Wants make life nicer but could go: takeaways, streaming, new clothes, holidays. Savings covers your emergency fund, goals, investing and paying off debt faster.

example.heading: An example
example.body: On £2,200 a month take-home, the rule gives £1,100 for needs, £660 for wants and £440 for savings. If rent and bills already cost £1,300, keeping £440 for savings leaves £460 for wants — so the squeeze falls on wants, not on your future.

caveats.heading: When the split doesn't fit
caveats.body: In much of the UK, rent alone can take more than half of take-home pay, especially in London. That doesn't mean budgeting has failed — treat 50/30/20 as a starting point. A 60/20/20 or 70/20/10 split is still a plan, as long as something goes to savings every month and you know where the rest goes.

faq.a1: A simple way to split take-home pay: 50% on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on savings and extra debt payments. It gives you a budget without tracking every category.
faq.q2: Is 50/30/20 based on gross or net pay?
faq.a2: Net — what actually arrives in your account after tax, National Insurance and pension contributions. If a workplace pension comes out of your pay, that's already saving, so the 20% is on top.
faq.q3: What if my needs are more than 50%?
faq.a3: It's common, especially when renting. Keep saving something, even if it's less than 20%, and let wants absorb most of the gap. Then look at the biggest fixed costs — rent, energy, phone and insurance — since one change there frees up money every month.
faq.q4: Do debt repayments count as needs or savings?
faq.a4: Minimum payments are needs: you have to make them. Anything above the minimum counts as savings, because it improves your finances just like putting money aside.
